subject: feminism
title: First Wave (c. 1848–1920): who got to count as a “woman” in public
dek: Suffrage, splits, and the people the word “we” left out.

thumb.alt: Carte-de-visite of Sojourner Truth, standing with a cane, spectacles, and a white cap, 1864.

hero.alt: Inez Milholland in a white cape on a white horse at the Woman Suffrage Procession, Washington, D.C., 3 March 1913. A crowd lines the street; the print is captioned Suffrage parade 3/3/13.
hero.caption: Inez Milholland leading the Woman Suffrage Procession, Washington, D.C., 3 March 1913 — the day before Woodrow Wilson’s inauguration. The image is the one the procession wanted at its head. The crowd, and who was allowed in the line, is the rest of the story.

honesty: “First wave” is a later Anglo-American label, not a name the people in this capsule used for themselves. It is useful as a frame — a span of public fights over whether women counted as political persons — and incomplete as a history. What follows uses the frame, then looks at the same decades elsewhere.

glossary.explain: English common-law doctrine that a married woman’s legal identity was “covered” by her husband’s. Property, contracts, and wages were his unless a statute carved out an exception.

A nineteenth-century middle-class story: men in public/economic life, women in the home as a moral climate. It was a class rule as much as a sex rule. Wage-earning and enslaved women were never offered that delicacy.

Village in western New York. On 19–20 July 1848 a convention there issued the Declaration of Sentiments. “Seneca Falls” later became shorthand for the start of organized U.S. women’s rights — a useful date, not the only origin.
The 1848 Seneca Falls text, modeled on the Declaration of Independence. It listed grievances including the vote. The vote was not the only demand, and not everyone in the room wanted it named first.
Ratified 1870. It barred denying the vote “on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.” It did not mention sex. The omission split the U.S. women’s-rights coalition.
Women’s Social and Political Union, founded 1903 by Emmeline Pankhurst. The militant wing of British suffrage: window-breaking, hunger strikes, and, in reply, force-feeding.
The system of legal racial segregation and disenfranchisement in the U.S. South after Reconstruction — poll taxes, literacy tests, violence. The Nineteenth Amendment did not repeal it.
Chinese Women’s Journal, edited by Qiu Jin in Shanghai in 1907. Two issues appeared. It argued for women’s education and against bound feet in the same breath as anti-Qing politics.
A small albumen photograph mounted on card, cheap to reproduce, sold and collected in the 1860s. Sojourner Truth sold hers with a printed caption and a copyright in her own name.

Frances Dana Gage. In 1863 she published a version of Sojourner Truth’s 1851 Akron speech that includes the refrain “Ain’t I a woman?” Contemporary 1851 newspaper accounts do not use the refrain that way.
Ratified 1920. It says the right to vote shall not be denied on account of sex. It did not touch poll taxes, literacy tests, or the violence that still blocked many Black women in the South.

In British prisons, hunger-striking suffragettes were restrained and fed through a tube. The Liberal government presented it as medical care. Militants presented it as assault. Both descriptions circulated in the press.
A later weather report for U.S. organized feminism in the 1920s–1950s: the vote arrived, the coalition thinned. It describes one organized current going quiet. It does not mean the questions ended.

American suffrage organizer, trained with British militants, then with Lucy Burns planned the 3 March 1913 Woman Suffrage Procession in Washington. Later the National Woman’s Party and the Equal Rights Amendment.

fun_fact.title: She copyrighted the shadow
fun_fact.text: In 1864 Sojourner Truth registered the copyright on her own cartes-de-visite in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan — unusual for a sitter; the photographer usually claimed the image. The cards were printed “I sell the shadow to support the substance.” She sold them at lectures because lectures did not pay enough. The existing portrait in this capsule is one of those cards.

sections.title: Covered, separate, and already in training

blocks.text: English common law treated a married woman as legally covered by her husband. The doctrine is called coverture. Her property, her contracts, her wages — the law did not see a separate person there. A single woman had more legal room; marriage closed it.

Industrial work left the house. What remained, for middle-class white women, was a story about respectability: the home as a moral climate, the woman as domestic, delicate, and good. Historians call this “separate spheres.” It was a rule of class as much as of sex. Enslaved women, and women who worked for wages, were never offered that delicacy. They were already in public — as labor, as property, as exceptions the ideology did not have to explain.

Abolition was the school many United States feminists came out of. They learned to petition, to lecture, to edit, to organize a room. The skills transferred. The alliance later cracked, when the question became which emancipation would be allowed to go first.

sections.title: A public “we,” and the people it could not hold

blocks.text: In 1848, at Seneca Falls, New York, a convention issued a Declaration of Sentiments modeled on the Declaration of Independence. The vote was among the grievances — not the only one, and not, at first, the one everyone in the room wanted named. The document still did something plain: it put women into the grammar of rights.

blocks.alt: Printed souvenir card titled Our Roll of Honor, listing women who signed the 1848 Declaration of Sentiments.
blocks.caption: A 1908 souvenir “Our Roll of Honor,” printed sixty years after Seneca Falls, listing the women who signed the 1848 Declaration of Sentiments. Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton head the first column. This is a commemorative card, not the 1848 manuscript.

blocks.text: In 1851 Sojourner Truth spoke at a women’s rights meeting in Akron, Ohio. The famous refrain “Ain’t I a woman?” comes from Frances Dana Gage’s 1863 rewrite of that speech. Contemporary 1851 newspaper accounts do not use the refrain that way. The later version is the one that traveled. The historical point does not depend on the catchphrase. A feminism built on white middle-class delicacy treats enslaved women and working women as exceptions — bodies that have already been asked to do too much to count as the “woman” the movement is picturing.

After the Civil War the coalition split over the Fifteenth Amendment (1870), which barred denying the vote “on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.” It did not mention sex. Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony opposed ratifying without women. Lucy Stone and Frederick Douglass would not block Black men’s suffrage in order to wait. The argument was about sequence, and about who was being asked to stand aside.

In Britain the movement divided by method: constitutional suffragists on one side, the militant Women’s Social and Political Union — Emmeline Pankhurst’s WSPU — on the other. Hunger strikes. Force-feeding. In 1913 Emily Wilding Davison died after stepping onto the course at the Epsom Derby.

blocks.alt: Formal seated portrait of Emmeline Pankhurst, 1913.
blocks.caption: Emmeline Pankhurst in 1913, the year Davison died at Epsom and the WSPU’s militancy was impossible to ignore. Constitutional suffragists were still collecting signatures. Pankhurst’s organization was collecting prison time.

blocks.text: On 3 March 1913, the day before Wilson’s inauguration, Alice Paul and Lucy Burns organized the Woman Suffrage Procession in Washington, D.C. Inez Milholland rode in white on a white horse. Ida B. Wells was told that Black women should march in a rear contingent. She refused, and stepped into the Illinois delegation as it passed.

blocks.alt: A dense crowd lining Pennsylvania Avenue to watch the 1913 woman suffrage procession in Washington, D.C.
blocks.caption: The crowd on Pennsylvania Avenue, 3 March 1913. Men climbed poles and wagons to see. The procession was designed to be unmissable on the eve of an inauguration. Unmissable is not the same as welcomed: the parade was repeatedly broken by spectators stepping into the street.

blocks.alt: Color official program cover for the Woman Suffrage Procession, Washington, D.C., 3 March 1913, showing a woman on horseback before the Capitol.
blocks.caption: The official program for the same day. The horse, the banner, the Capitol: a picture of who the procession wanted to look like. Wells’s decision to leave the “rear contingent” is the part the program does not print.

blocks.text: The Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in 1920. It did not undo Jim Crow. Many Black women in the South were still blocked by poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence. The amendment changed the federal text. The ground did not change with it.

The same years, elsewhere: Qiu Jin 秋瑾 (1875–1907). She unbound her feet, studied in Japan, edited 中國女報 (the Chinese Women’s Journal), and was executed after the 1907 Anqing uprising. Her public life does not sit on the Anglo-American staircase from Seneca Falls to 1920. It belongs in the same decades anyway — a woman deciding she would count in public, under a different state, and paying for it.

sections.title: Four lives the frame has to stretch for

people.name: Sojourner Truth
people.alt: 1864 carte-de-visite of Sojourner Truth standing with a cane. Printed caption: I sell the shadow to support the substance.
people.caption: Carte-de-visite, 1864. “I sell the shadow to support the substance.”
people.text: Born enslaved in New York. She sold cartes-de-visite captioned “I sell the shadow to support the substance.” The card was a living. It was also an argument about who owned the image of a woman who had been treated as property.

people.name: Ida B. Wells
people.alt: Studio portrait of Ida B. Wells-Barnett by Mary Garrity, about 1893.
people.caption: Ida B. Wells-Barnett, photograph by Mary Garrity, c. 1893.
people.text: Anti-lynching journalist; Southern Horrors appeared in 1892. She treated suffrage and racial terror as one fight, which is why a segregated parade order was not a small slight. She walked into the Illinois line instead.

people.name: Inez Milholland
people.alt: Inez Milholland on a white horse in the 1913 suffrage procession, Washington, D.C.
people.caption: The 1913 visual: white cape, white horse, Pennsylvania Avenue.
people.text: Lawyer and the image the 1913 procession needed at its head. She died in 1916 on a western suffrage tour, at thirty. The photograph outlived the campaign she was riding for.

people.name: Qiu Jin 秋瑾
people.alt: Portrait of Qiu Jin, photographed in the last years of the Qing dynasty, between 1900 and 1907.
people.caption: Qiu Jin, photographed between 1900 and 1907.
people.text: Unbound feet. Study in Japan. Editor of 中國女報. Executed after the 1907 Anqing uprising. If “first wave” cannot hold her, the phrase is too small — not her life.

blocks.alt: Sojourner Truth’s 1864 carte-de-visite, with the printed line I sell the shadow to support the substance under her portrait.
blocks.caption: Sojourner Truth, 1864. She sold the card because lectures did not pay enough. She also put her own copyright on it.

blocks.text: Truth sold her image because lectures did not pay enough. The “shadow” is the photograph — a thing that can be reproduced, captioned, passed from hand to hand. The “substance” is the work, and the body that had been treated as property. She put the sentence on the card in English, under her own name, and made the sale part of the argument: I will be paid for the copy of me that you can hold.
Keep the card in mind when a movement talks about “women” as if the category were already settled. Someone is always deciding which body is the subject, and which body is the illustration.

sections.title: The vote, the doldrums, and the staircase

blocks.text: In the United States the 1920s through the 1950s are often called the “doldrums”: the vote arrived, the coalition thinned. The word is a weather report written after the fact. It describes a particular organized feminism going quiet. It does not mean the questions ended.

What gets called the second wave — the 1960s and 1970s — turned to the workplace, to sexuality, to housework. “The personal is political.” The who-counts problem returned in public, including in the Combahee River Collective statement of 1977, which refused to treat race, sex, and class as separate queues.

The wave metaphor itself is the after. It offers a tidy staircase: first the vote, then the rest. It hides the people who were never on the stairs — and the fights that did not wait for the next numbered swell.
When a movement says “we,” who is being asked to wait?
